concept: Why do starlings fly in huge swirling flocks without crashing?
title: Murmuration Sky
tagline: Hundreds turn as one, but no one leads.

science.hiddenLaw: Leaderless flocking emerges from three local interaction rules applied to only the ~6-7 nearest neighbors: short-range separation (repulsion to avoid crowding/collisions), intermediate-range alignment (steer toward neighbors' average heading), and long-range cohesion (steer toward neighbors' average position) — with no global information, no leader, and no choreographed plan.
science.plainStatement: Starlings don't follow a leader. Each bird watches just its 6-7 closest neighbors and follows three simple rules: keep a little distance, fly the same direction, and stay near the group. The huge swirling flock pattern emerges on its own from those local rules.
misconceptions: A lead bird at the front directs the flock and others follow it — so without a leader the flock would be disordered.
Each bird needs to see or know what the entire flock is doing to stay coordinated.
Birds avoid mid-air crashes by planning long-range trajectories or communicating across the flock, not by simple short-range repulsion from immediate neighbors.

sources.title: Reynolds, C.W. (1987). Flocks, herds and schools: A distributed behavioral model. SIGGRAPH '87.
Ballerini et al. (2008). Interaction ruling animal collective behavior depends on topological rather than metric distance: Evidence from a field study. PNAS 105(4).
Couzin, I.D. et al. (2002). Collective memory and spatial sorting in animal groups. Journal of Theoretical Biology 218(1).

story.setting: Dusk over the marsh. Thousands of dark specks swirl and fold like smoke.
story.mystery: How does a thousand-bird cloud twist without a single collision?
story.goal: Tweak the flock's instincts and watch what holds the dance together.

predictions.prompt: What keeps birds from crashing into each other mid-air?
options: A short push away from close neighbors
Planning long routes across the whole flock

predictions.prompt: How do hundreds of birds end up flying the same way?
options: Each copies direction of a few nearby birds
A front bird steers everyone else
Each watches the entire flock at once

predictions.prompt: What keeps the flock from drifting apart and scattering?
options: A gentle pull toward nearby neighbors
Each bird tracks the flock's center
The leader herds stragglers back in

transfer.setup: A swarm of 300 reef drones must move as a group with no central control. Each drone only senses its 7 closest neighbors.
transfer.question: If drones stop copying neighbors' headings, what happens to the swarm?

checks.description: With separation active, collision rate stays near zero despite high density and alignment/cohesion.
Control: removing separation (weight=0) while keeping alignment and cohesion causes collisions to appear.
With alignment active, flock becomes highly polarized (all flying same direction) from random start.
Control: removing alignment (weight=0) destroys polarization even with separation and cohesion present.
With cohesion active, flock remains compact with small mean radius around centroid.
Control: removing cohesion (weight=0) causes flock radius to grow/fragment over time.
